chunks: "Not immediately, and for a motor usually not at all.
The coil resistance is 1 ohm, so 12 amps is the limit the current approaches, V over R, but a coil is an inductor, so the current starts at zero and rises with time constant L over R.
With a few millihenries that's a few milliseconds, so I'd see roughly 63 percent of 12 amps after one time constant and over 99 percent after five. When would I see 12 amps?
For a solenoid on DC, once the transient is over, in steady state, because the inductor then drops no voltage and only the 1 ohm limits the current.
That's 144 watts in the coil, so it won't survive long.
For a motor, only when it's stalled, because as it spins it generates a back-EMF and the current is V minus K e omega over R. At speed it might be half an amp. When wouldn't I?
At the instant of turn-on, since the inductor holds the current at zero. With a spinning motor, because of back-EMF. On AC, since the inductive reactance adds to the impedance.
If the supply, wires, switch or MOSFET add resistance, the current is less than 12 amps. If the coil heats up, copper resistance rises, 0.
4 percent per kelvin, so 12 amps becomes about 9. And with PWM, the average is duty times that."
